articles.title: Tata Harrier EV breaks down repeatedly within months; refund of Rs 27.98 lakh along with Rs 65,000 payout ordered
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Hyderabad district consumer commission has directed Tata Select Motors to take back a Tata Harrier EV and refund its price after deduct.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Hyderabad district consumer commission has directed Tata Select Motors to take back a Tata Harrier EV and refund its price after deducting 10 percent depreciation, after finding that the vehicle repeatedly developed smart-key and central-locking problems despite repairs. The commission also awarded Rs 50,000 compensation and Rs 15,000 costs to the buyer, but declined to award the punitive damages sought. The order was passed on September 7, 2026.Why did the buyer approach the consumer commission?According to the commission order, M/s Refrigeration Equipment and Solutions, a partnership firm represented by partner Pawan Bagrecha, purchased a Tata Harrier EV Empowered + 75 APC from Tata Select Motors on August 1, 2025, for Rs 27.98 lakh. The vehicle was partly financed through a loan.Within days of delivery, the complainant alleged that the car repeatedly failed to start and developed problems with smart-key connectivity and central locking. The complaint said the issue occurred four times within a month and the vehicle had stopped midway on multiple occasions.The dealer allegedly attributed the initial problem to a software glitch. The complainant later sought replacement of the vehicle, alleging that the problems continued despite repeated complaints and repairs. The complainant had sought a refund of Rs 29,29,395, along with Rs 10 lakh as compensation for mental agony and harassment and a further Rs 10 lakh as punitive damages to penalise the dealer for alleged gross negligence and unfair trade practices.The dealer denied deficiency in service and argued that no manufacturing defect had been proved through an expert or automobile engineer's report. It also said it was only an authorised dealer and service centre, and that the manufacturer had not been made a party. The dealer maintained that it had responded promptly, resolved the software issue through an update and replaced the lock under warranty.What did the commission observe?The bench of President B Uma Venkata Subba Lakshmi and members C Lakshmi Prasanna and B Raji Reddy examined the communications, job cards and service history produced by both sides. The coommission found that the buyer had reported the smart-key and central-locking problems within days of purchase and that the dealer had acknowledged them."On perusal of the record, it is evident from the reply communication dated 21st August at Ex.A6 that the complainant has reported the issue of smart key out-of-range issue and the central locking system malfunction within days of purchase of the subject vehicle and the reported complaints are acknowledged by the personnel of the opposite party. It is further evident from the communication chats between the parties at Ex.A5 & Ex.A6 that the complainant's vehicle has stopped midway and the complainant has called the opposite party to report the issue," the commission observed.The service history showed repeated complaints, including inability to lock or unlock the vehicle and starting problems. The commission said the dealer had not provided an explanation for the cause of the problems and the issues persisted even after repairs."Also, there is no iota of material to show the date of delivery of the vehicle from the manufacturer to the dealer. In the absence of material evidence, it cannot be said that the dealer is not liable if a defective vehicle is delivered to the customer. The question of expert evidence does not arise in the present case as the service history/job card submitted by the opposite party and the complainant establishes that the reported issues of smart key out-of-range issue and the central locking system malfunction persist even after filing the consumer complaint and the vehicle of the complainant has stopped mid-way," the commission said.It held that the evidence established that the reported problems persisted and answered the issue of deficiency in service in favour of the complainant.The commission said the dealer, which had executed the sale, was liable to refund the vehicle's price after deducting 10 percent depreciation. It said the buyer was also entitled to reasonable compensation because the vehicle had been purchased through a loan."Admittedly, the complainant has purchased the vehicle by taking loan. Hence, the complainant is entitled for reasonable compensation and costs for the mental agony and financial hardship suffered by him," the commission noted.The commission observed that awarding compensation as high as the Rs 10 lakh sought would result in inequity, noting that just compensation is meant to be fair and equitable and "not intended to be a bonanza, largesse or source of profit." It awarded Rs 50,000 compensation and Rs 15,000 costs, and did not award any punitive damages.The commission directed the dealer to refund the amount after deducting 10 percent depreciation from Rs 26,64,761.90, against return of the vehicle. The order is to be complied with within 45 days. In case of default, the refund amount will carry 9 percent annual interest from the date of the order until payment.

articles.title: Carlota Ciganda’s passion fueled Europe’s Solheim Cup win: ‘I love beating the Americans’
articles.summary: CROMVOIRT, Netherlands — “I’m not going to bed, I’m just going crazy,” Carlota Ciganda said, standing on the 18th green, her European blue shirt a few shades...
articles.body:
CROMVOIRT, Netherlands — "I'm not going to bed, I'm just going crazy," Carlota Ciganda said, standing on the 18th green, her European blue shirt a few shades darker, stained by champagne.

The Spaniard is from Pamplona, the city best known for where they run with bulls, and she found herself at the heart of the drama all weekend, her fire antagonizing the United States and leading Team Europe. It was only fitting then that Ciganda was the one who officially brought the Solheim Cup back to Europe, beating a newfound nemesis, 4&2, for the decisive point.

"Mrs. Solheim Cup," Nelly Korda said as she congratulated Ciganda after Europe's 15-13 win over the U.S.

Ciganda, who hit the decisive shot in 2023 when Europe retained the Solheim Cup, is an eight-time veteran with a 5-2-1 record in singles. In her match against Jennifer Kupcho she had already clinched at least a half-point, meaning it was actually LPGA breakout star Lottie Woad who got to unknowingly hole the Cup winner in her match against Auston Kim.

Woad, the world No. 7, had been paired with world No. 8 Charley Hull in four matches over the first two days by Europe's captain Anna Nordqvist. That turned out to be an ongoing concern all weekend as the all-English partnership lost three times and produced just half a point. But it was Hull who earned the first point of Sunday singles, putting Europe in the lead. The European stars bullishly delivered all day. Besides the aforementioned trio, Linn Grant (4-0-0 this week), Nastasia Nadaud (3-1), Nanna Koerstz Madsen (3&2 over Andrea Lee) and Julia López Ramírez (3&2 over Yealimi Noh) all earned full points.

"Europe's on fire, USA is terrified," shouted Woad, draped in an England flag with compatriot and fellow rookie Mimi Rhodes. Swirling around them was a melee of cameras, celebrations and commiserations. The U.S. team had to cut through Europe's excitement to offer congratulations to their rivals, who did pause their beer-swilling antics to accept what was a true graciousness in defeat.

As "Sweet Caroline" by Neil Diamond blared out from the speakers on the first tee, the Europeans headed back to where the fun began on Friday morning. And to be reunited with their jubilant fans who had made it an incredible and raucous occasion for both teams across all three days.

That Diamond song, a staple anthem at sporting events, is what vice-captain Mel Reid said — or tried to say with a lost voice — helped find Europe a way out of their low mood on Saturday evening. Ciganda and Céline Boutier were 2 up with two holes to go in the final match Saturday evening, when Kupcho made a 92-foot putt on the 17th followed by one from 29 feet on No. 18 to win the full point alongside Lindy Duncan and ensure Day 2 ended in a tie, 8-8.

The putts were huge in distance and momentum. And when the final one went in, Kupcho cupped her ear in the direction of Ciganda and screamed "vamos", a clear reference to what Ciganda had shouted a day before, when she somehow won a half-point with a messy up-and-down on the 18th hole against Korda and Lauren Coughlin.

By chance (opposing captains release their lineups without knowing the other's), Ciganda and Kupcho were paired against each other on Sunday. For Ciganda, that meant only one thing — revenge.

"I was really happy to see that I was playing against Kupcho," Ciganda said. "She's a fighter, I'm a fighter, and I told her, 'Look, great playing'. I mean, even yesterday what she did was amazing on 17 and 18. But today I knew she had no chance. I was like, I want to kill you."

What had also lifted Ciganda and Europe when they got back to the team hotel on Saturday was a message sent directly to Ciganda from compatriot and Ryder Cup legend José María Olazábal. And there was "Sweet Caroline" put on over the speakers in the team room.

"I just felt like it just changed the mood and united us. It was weird, we just forgot what happened, the disappointment, and we just got back on it," European vice-captain Mel Reid said.

Olazábal may have captained the "Miracle at Medinah," but Europe needed no fairytale comeback on Sunday. It did need heart and passion, the kind of which was served up and best exemplified by Ciganda.

"I love this week. As I said, I love playing for the team, for my teammates, for everyone here," Ciganda said. "… I just love it. I mean, I love beating the Americans. And then, yeah, just winning for Team Europe, it's the best feeling."

As Europe's giddy and gallant team danced on the first tee while waiting for their trophy to be presented to them by John Solheim, whose family founded the competition back in 1990, U.S. captain Angela Stanford pulled her team together for a photo on the 18th green. Beer bottle tops, champagne corks and a broken American dream each lay scattered.

"I can promise you this hurts more for them than maybe for us because they were the ones playing," Stanford said. "The good news is they can show back up in Kentucky in a couple of years and make it right."

The next Solheim Cup is in 2028 at Valhalla Golf Club in Louisville, Kentucky. Europe will come in having held the Cup after four of the last five editions.

As a cloud of blue and yellow smoke exploded into the air behind them, Nordqvist lifted the trophy in front of her entire family, who had traveled in from Sweden to witness the crowning moment of a career that lasted almost two decades and saw her win three majors.

And that is when the rain, which had been off but mostly on all day, began to fall on Europe's stage, a place where there was to be no American parade.

On Saturday, Stanford ran onto the team bus with a crate of beers for her team in hand. Some wondered if they celebrated too soon. But Stanford defended her actions after Kupcho's heroics. "You don't want to take away from those moments," Stanford said. "We're never going to see anything like that again."

Perhaps not, but on Sunday night as Europe loaded the bus for the trip back to their lodgings , team helper Dame Laura Davies, who won four Solheim Cups as a player and three as a vice-captain, appeared with a case of Heinekens.

articles.title: Keeping farming soil healthy in times of drought
articles.summary: A grower from Cornwall says soil, density of crop, a good irrigation have protected him in drought.
articles.body:
It has been a summer of record-breaking temperatures, heatwaves, drought and hosepipe bans, leaving many farmers and growers struggling.

But one grower near St Columb, Cornwall, who operates a small-scale market garden, has been relatively unaffected by the drought, he has said.

Conor Kendrew has set up an irrigation system that uses a spring, a pond and any collected rain water and, because the site is 0.5 acre (0.2 hectare), sprinklers can reach a large part of the crop.

Kendrew said: "We invested very very heavily from the outset on a very good irrigation system. We could probably push pressure that is about six times what people's houses are sitting at, which means we can make it rain."

Kendrew said prepping the ground for drought resilience was the single most important thing to do.

He said he used a lot of compost and did minimal cultivation where the residual crop was always mown and put back into the ground.

He said: "We are building soil organic matter and soil organic carbon all the time.

"The whole farm is powered by solar energy as well, so we've got the free water but we've also got the free energy. I'm not a grower who staring at a massively inflated electric or water bill each month.

"We've [also] set up an off-grid resilient system.

"We all kind of know climate change is coming.

I think, perhaps, I and my wife Rose have had a little bit more of an idea how real it is going to get quite quickly, so we've prepared for it.

"To say we're OK for water isn't to say everything has been a breeze.

"The heat itself stresses crops out tremendously, no matter how wet they are.

"Like everyone, I am shocked [at recent weather and heatwaves], but, like an engineer, you would sort of over design your system for this sort of thing."

articles.title: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel, citing a global shortage
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average. Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, removing supplies from the already tight global market. But the global crunch also came after the war on Iran curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm elections in November. Trump was asked by a reporter if he had spoken with Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He responded by calling on Zelenskyy to halt strikes against Russia. “Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open, which is being played at his Doonbeg golf club. “We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world,” he said. According to a report published Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February. “Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the IEA wrote. It added that in February, combined next exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf and Russia “accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade.” Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow’s more than four-year-old invasion of Ukraine. Russia has ramped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce Ukraine’s defenses. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralize civilians. Civilians were killed and injured overnight into Sunday as Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes. Two people were killed and 14 more wounded near an oil and industrial hub in Russia’s Tatarstan, according to local officials, while Ukrainian authorities reported on Russian drones pummeling the Black Sea port of Odesa and starting a fire near a border crossing with Poland. The two Russian civilians died after a drone slammed into a tree near their parked car in the city of Nizhnekamsk, according to the office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov. Nizhnekamsk houses a key cluster of oil refineries and other industrial plants. Mayor Radmir Belyaev said that a fire had broken out at an unspecified “enterprise.” Ukraine also claimed to have hit a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, in Russia’s Krasnodar region near Crimea. The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) agency said its drones struck a key oil processing unit and the refinery’s tank farm overnight into Sunday. Krasnodar authorities said the strike on “an enterprise” in Slavyansk-on-Kuban injured three people and damaged an oil pipeline. Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, Russia’s defense ministry said Sunday. In Ukraine, at least nine people were injured in a “massive” Russian nighttime attack on Odesa, according to Serhii Lysak from the city’s military administration. Odesa is home to Ukraine’s main port hub on the Black Sea and has faced sustained drone and missile strikes, with Kyiv accusing Moscow of trying to choke off its exports. A Russian drone attack on Saturday struck a residential high-rise in Odesa, killing two people and injuring 26 others, Ukrainian officials said. Russian overnight strikes also pounded western Ukraine, though there were no immediate reports of casualties. One drone set fire to a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland, according to Ukraine’s top diplomat and a spokesperson for the local customs force. “This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X. Ukraine’s border crossings with Poland are a conduit for much of the military and humanitarian aid sent by Western allies. Valentyna Chernysh, a spokesperson for the Volyn Customs Office, told The Associated Press that the Yahodyn crossing was intact and no one was harmed. Earlier this week, two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday. The following day a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point was avoided due to the cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, according to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ukraine’s air force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 409 Russian drones of various types overnight, including a newer jet-powered version that is faster and more difficult to intercept. It said Russia had attacked Ukraine with 453 drones in total.

articles.title: After a $2.4 billion money laundering bust, Singapore now has hundreds of luxury handbags to shift
articles.summary: In a high-security storage facility, Singaporean officials have so many forfeited luxury items that it will take nine months to auction them off.
articles.body: One of history’s largest ever money laundering busts left officials in Singapore with a multibillion-dollar question: What to do with the cars, properties and thousands of luxury goods seized in the investigation? Three years after the coordinated raids, which saw over 400 police officers target a criminal network profiting from scams and illicit gambling, the answer is now partly on display deep inside a secretive storage facility near the affluent city-state’s airport. In a windowless, concrete-walled room, collectors are being invited to browse hundreds of the forfeited items. Cartier rings, Bulgari necklaces and Hermès “Kelly” bracelets are on show alongside rows of handbags and accessories by brands like Chanel and Louis Vuitton. It’s a haul so vast that the sales are being spread across 15 auctions, between now and next May, to avoid flooding the market. “The amount of luxury handbags, the sheer volume of the jewelry here — all of great quality and all from the best jewelry houses — is something we don’t see every day,” said Christopher Lanigan-O’Keeffe, co-founder of Hotlotz, the auction house tasked with selling the goods. “You might be lucky to see one or two pieces like this, but all together at once is quite unusual,” he said as he toured CNN around the viewing room in Singapore’s high-security Freeport. Conducted after two years of investigations, the country-wide police operation involved assets worth more than $3 billion Singaporean dollars ($2.4 billion). As well as cash, cryptocurrency and gold bars, officers seized properties, sports cars, wine, liquor, electronics and even hundreds of Bearbricks, collectible Japanese teddy toys that can sell for six-figure sums. Ten Chinese nationals (although many held passports issued by other countries including Cambodia and Turkey) were later convicted on charges including money laundering and forgery. The culprits owned businesses and properties in Singapore, where prosecutors said they channeled the proceeds of overseas criminal activities. They were each jailed for between 13 and 17 months, though all have since been released and deported. Forfeited luxury items were also linked to 17 suspects who remain on the run overseas, 15 of whom agreed to surrender assets to Singapore in return for having Interpol notices against them withdrawn. Some objects going up for auction carry evidence of their illicit past. An 18-karat gold ring, for instance, is engraved with the initials “SHJ,” matching those of Su Haijin, one of the convicted men. But most of the objects are in good or pristine condition, indistinguishable from equivalent items on the resale market. Hotlotz has valued them as such. The auction house’s first two sales, which run online until later this month, are expected to raise up to 3.9 million Singapore dollars ($3.1 million), with proceeds going directly to Singapore’s treasury. Lanigan-O’Keeffe believes the objects’ origins will have little impact on the final prices. “Each individual collector or buyer will have their own views on that,” he said. “To some people, maybe (it matters), but to other people, some of these items are hard to come by.” Hermès by the hundreds The sales have been over a year in the making. In July 2025, Singapore appointed Deloitte to liquidate the non-cash assets seized by investigators. The accounting firm then selected four real estate firms — SRI, Knight Frank, Edmund Tie & Company and List International Realty — to auction or sell more than 80 properties. Among them is a four-bedroom penthouse in the Norman Foster-designed South Beach development that is expected to sell for upwards of 25.3 million Singapore dollars ($20 million) later this month. Hotlotz, meanwhile, was asked to recuperate as much money as possible from the luxury goods. The auction house has spent the last four months authenticating and valuing the haul. The items “would not be out of place in any of the top auctions in New York, London, Paris or Hong Kong,” said Lanigan-O’Keeffe, adding: “To be able to offer the caliber of these goods in one series is quite unheard of.” The highest estimate belongs to a 15-carat yellow diamond ring that Hotlotz predicts will sell for up to 300,000 Singapore dollars ($237,000). Rings by Hermès and British jeweler Graff are also expected to attract six-figure sums. Elsewhere, a pumpkin handbag, from Louis Vuitton’s collaboration with the late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, has already exceeded auction estimates, with a current top bid of 39,000 Singapore dollars ($31,000) at the time of publication. Other lots span diamond-studded belts, hair clips and even children’s jewelry — small anklets, rings and bracelets made from solid gold — once owned by suspects in the case. Future sales will feature luxury watches and enough Hermès handbags (around 250, Hotlotz said) for two standalone auctions, the first of which is scheduled for November. By holding the auctions online, Hotlotz hopes to attract bidders from around the world, not just Singapore. And with estimates starting as low as 120 Singapore dollars ($95), for a Miu Miu ring or a Gucci hair clip, these items aren’t just for the ultra-wealthy. “The most expensive things aren’t always the most interesting,” Lanigan-O’Keeffe said.

articles.title: Leading Cuban dissidents see Trump as best shot at change, but want a bigger role
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s pressure campaign on Cuba is probably the best chance for collapsing the country’s repressive, communist regime, high-profile Cuban political activists and survivors of the regime’s prisons told The Hill. But more effort needs to be given to including the Cuban opposition and democratic movement, they added. José Daniel Ferrer, a leading Cuban…
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s pressure campaign on Cuba is probably the best chance for collapsing the country’s repressive, communist regime, high-profile Cuban political activists and survivors of the regime’s prisons told The Hill.

But more effort needs to be given to including the Cuban opposition and democratic movement, they added.

José Daniel Ferrer, a leading Cuban political activist exiled in Miami, and Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara, released in July after five years in a Cuban prison after direct intervention from the U.S., spoke to The Hill last week ahead of their acceptance of the freedom of speech award from the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), a pro-democracy organization funded by Congress.

“This is perhaps the best chance that something will occur,” Ferrer, who was also released from prison in Cuba in October 2025 after demands from the U.S., said of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign.

He said the unprecedented efforts were buoyed by the high discontent among the Cuban people, organizing more than 1,000 spontaneous protests throughout the summer, rivaling the 2021 protest movement that triggered a brutal crackdown, including Ferrer’s arrest.

Alcántara, a prominent political artist, was also a victim of that crackdown. He was arrested in July of that year as a leader in the San Isidro Movement, a group of artists, journalists and activists demanding the right to freedom of speech, inspiring a mass protest movement under the slogan “patria y vida,” or “country and life,” a play on the communist revolutionary slogan “country or death.”

The Cuban government released Alcántara on July 18 under U.S. pressure but also forced him into exile — separating him from his family, friends and political community.

Alcántara said he is still recovering from his time in prison and getting used to the reality of life in exile, describing it as a clash of two sides of the Straits of Florida.

“I am still processing. It’s a difficult process, but I have to do it. Especially because we have to continue working and pushing to achieve freedom in Cuba,” he said.

The regime did not release Maykel “Osorbo” Castillo Pérez, another San Isidro Movement leader and musician, despite U.S. demands . Félix Navarro, a close political partner of Ferrer’s, is also still in jail.

Both men were honored with the NED award, and Alcántara spoke on behalf of his “brother” Pérez, growing visibly emotional.

“I want this award to serve as a monument; it should be engraved on the conscience of everyone here, of injustice being done to him,” he said.

“Today, there are decisions being made about Cuba, and in my opinion, the Cuban opposition, the Democratic movement, the independent artistic movement, is not being fully taken into account,” he told the crowd at Mount Vernon.

“This award will serve as a reminder that that sacrifice needs to be taken into account.”

President Trump said he believes he will have the “honor” of taking over Cuba , signaling his desire for a Venezuela-like relationship with the island that preserves the regime but with a leader compliant to U.S. demands.

Cubans are not necessarily against a U.S.-style intervention similar to the events of Jan. 3, when the American military descended on Caracas to snatch authoritarian President Nicolás Maduro and bring him to New York on an indictment of drug charges, according to Ferrer.

“People wish change so much that, after Jan. 3, many were wishing for something similar to what happened in Venezuela to happen as well in Cuba,” he said.

But negotiations over a possible exit of Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel have reportedly stalled. And even if the Trump administration succeeded in changing Cuba’s leadership, its record in Venezuela so far has included empowering Maduro’s vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, to lead the country and prioritizing U.S. control over the country’s oil fields.

Trump has boxed out María Corina Machado, whose party won the last Venezuelan presidential election, and instead hand-picked leaders among the democratic opposition to negotiate with the regime.

Prioritizing economic deals over democratic reforms appeared to be the initial U.S. strategy in Cuba, as well.

The Miami Herald reported Thursday that the U.S. sought control over Cuba’s energy infrastructure to allow American investment to rebuild it and benefit from the import and distribution of gasoline, while also demanding Díaz-Canel flee the island.

It’s not clear whom Trump wants to take power, although the administration has cultivated ties with Raúl Castro’s grandson Col. Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro. But the Herald reported that such talks collapsed and the administration has since ratcheted up its sanctions pressure — announcing new measures about every few weeks since May.

The Cuban government is looking to counteract those measures by imposing economic reforms to open the island up to foreign investment, USA Today reported .

Ferrer and Alcántara both called for the U.S. to internationalize its sanctions campaign on Cuba — bringing in partners from Europe, Latin America, Asia and even the African continent to truly isolate the regime and force change.

“This all stems from a deep understanding that the Cuban regime, without pressure, will not make concessions,” Ferrer said. “They need to be pressured; they need to understand that their behavior will not be tolerated, that there will be consequences.”

“We need their solidarity,” Alcántara said about the international community, citing the regime’s human rights abuses.

There are more than 1,300 political prisoners in Cuba, according to a recent report from Prisoners Defenders . The Trump administration imposed an effective fuel blockade on Cuba in January, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation. The population of about 8 million are facing shortages of food, water, electricity and fuel.

“Cuba is a DICTATORSHIP, with all capital letters,” Alcántara said. “It is the epitome of violations of human rights.”

Ferrer and Alcántara represent the diverse range of Cuba’s political opposition across generation, race and profession. Ferrer is a conventional, suit-wearing, Hispanic politician. Alcántara is the Afro-Cuban, casual and stylish artist. Alcántara said the NED award recognizes the importance of both their styles of political engagement.

Both men reflected on their long ties to the NED, where grants from the organization aided and sustained their political campaigning and organizing efforts.

“This award is a symbol of the unity across generations, across race and across geographic distances in Cuba in favor of democracy,” Alcántara said.

“And the different types of ways to do politics, and to engage in politics.”

articles.title: ‘Spirit of country is pluralism’: Owaisi hits back at Amit Shah’s UCC pledge, questions BJP allies’ independence
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Monday hit back at Union home minister Amit Shah’s announcement that BJP-led NDA governments in 21 stat.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Monday hit back at Union home minister Amit Shah’s announcement that BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states would implement the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) before 2029, questioning whether the BJP’s allies had an independent political voice.Owaisi said the allies should demonstrate that they were not merely “choti BJP”, while arguing that the UCC was not about equality but about targeting Muslims.In a post on X, Owaisi said the Law Commission appointed by the NDA government had concluded that a UCC was “neither necessary nor desirable” for India.Speaking to news agency ANI, Owaisi said the BJP was pursuing the UCC not for equality but to target Muslims. He alleged that the move was contrary to constitutional provisions including Articles 14, 25, 26 and 29.“The very soul and spirit of this country is pluralism,” Owaisi said, adding that he believed the BJP and RSS were attempting to impose Hindu law on non-Hindus.Owaisi challenges BJP to implement UCC in GoaOwaisi also challenged Shah, the BJP and RSS to implement in Goa the same UCC framework introduced in Uttarakhand, Gujarat and Assam.“Go ahead and implement it in Goa,” Owaisi said, referring to the BJP’s stated plans for the state. He questioned whether the party would actually introduce the same UCC there.Owaisi also cited provisions he said exist under Goa’s current legal framework, including provisions concerning second marriages in certain circumstances and exemptions relating to Catholic marriages and divorce proceedings.He said these provisions raised questions about the BJP’s argument for a uniform legal framework across religions.Owaisi targets ‘disturbed areas’, ‘love jihad’ lawsOwaisi also questioned the BJP’s support for the UCC while BJP-ruled states have laws such as the Disturbed Areas Act, which he said prevents Hindus and Muslims from freely transferring property between each other.“It’s ironic that the BJP wants a UCC while its own states pass laws like the Disturbed Areas Act, which prohibit the sale of property between Muslims and Hindus,” he said.Owaisi also referred to laws concerning “love jihad”, alleging that such provisions had been applied against Muslims and Christians.“A UCC isn’t about equality; it’s about targeting Muslims,” he said.Shah says UCC will be implemented before 2029Shah had on Sunday said BJP-led NDA governments in all 21 states under their rule would introduce the UCC before 2029.“We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code in several states, and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA-ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029,” Shah said in Mumbai.The UCC proposes a common set of personal laws covering matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption, irrespective of religion.Owaisi also drew a parallel with the controversy surrounding the National Register of Citizens (NRC) and the anti-CAA/NRC protests of 2019.He alleged that Shah’s “misplaced arrogance” and “chronology” had contributed to the protests and recalled that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had clarified at the time that no NRC was going to be implemented.Owaisi said a similar situation was now unfolding around the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, which he alleged had caused hardship, particularly to minorities, SC/STs and migrants.He warned that an NRC would be “100 times worse” and referred to the experience in Assam.“The National Register of Citizens will force everyone to stand in line and prove their citizenship. In a country where 80 crore people depend on ration for food, you want them to find documents and prove their citizenship?” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Thousands demand end to violence in Mexican cartel hotspot
articles.summary: The city has seen violence skyrocket since a feud broke out between two rival factions of the Sinaloa cartel.
articles.body:
Thousands of people have taken to the streets of Culiacán to demand an end to the violence that has wracked the north Mexico city.

The state of Sinaloa has seen the number of murders and disappearances skyrocket since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel started a bloody war two years ago.

Residents dressed in white held up posters of missing loved and signs reading "We don't want fear, we want peace" at the protest on Sunday.

More than three million people live in Sinaloa and many say that the war between the two rival factions - known as Los Chapitos and La Mayiza - has blighted their lives.

'Fear is everywhere': BBC reports from Mexican city turned into war zone by drug cartel feud

The march was scheduled to coincide with the second anniversary since the start of the conflict - which feud broke out after the arrest of wanted drug lord Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada in the US.

His followers, La Mayiza, allege he was betrayed by the son of the infamous founder of the Sinaloa cartel, Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán, and have turned on members of his faction, Los Chapitos.

The two factions regularly carry out ambushes, drive-by shootings and erect roadblocks by hijacking trucks, which they set alight.

Residents of Culiacán have been caught up in this internecine war.

Not only has the number of murders and disappearances shot up in the state but also those of extortions and robberies, official figures suggest.

Sunday's protest was organised by relatives of victims, local businesses, civil society groups and the Catholic church.

Businessman Sergio Esquer told AFP news agency that more than 5,000 businesses had closed since the start of the feud.

"That's the tragedy Sinaloa is experiencing," Esquer, who is a leader in the centre-left opposition party Movimiento Ciudadano, said.

The event started with a Mass in which the bishop of Culiacán called on members of the warring groups to put an end to their violence.

"Stop, look at what's happening, look at the affected families, look at the young people and at our city. No amount of power, of money, territory or ambition is worth more than a human life," he said.

Among those who attended the protest were relatives of a one-year-old boy who died after being hit by a bullet in the head during a shootout in the city last week.

As well as the wave of violence, Sinaloa state has also been hit by political upheaval in recent months.

In April, US prosecutors accused the state's governor, Rubén Rocha, and nine other current and former officials of conspiring with Los Chapitos to smuggle drugs into the US.

Rocha, who has denied any wrongdoing, stepped down temporarily while Mexican prosecutors opened an investigation of their own into the allegations.

Three weeks ago, he returned to his post, but just days later requested another leave of absence after President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on social media, without directly naming him that "power without principles becomes arrogance".

articles.summary: Tech News News: When Bill Gates started constructing his Median estate, famously known as Xanadu 2.0, in 1990, he encountered an unexpected challenge: the northen spo.
articles.body: When Bill Gates started constructing his Median estate, famously known as Xanadu 2.0, in 1990, he encountered an unexpected challenge: the northen spotted owl crises. The mansion, designed in Pacific Lodge style and sprawling across 66,000 square feet, was initially planned to use old‑growth timber. But with the owl listed as a threatened species, America banned the use of wood from old‑growth habitats. Architect James Cutler, known for his environmental stance, also opposed felling living old‑growth trees.Instead of pushing through, Gates compromised. He funded what Cutler described as the world’s first heavy‑timber‑recycling sawmill, sourcing reclaimed wood through Ferndale‑based G.R. Plume & Company. Half a million board feet of salvaged Douglas fir beams from Long‑Bell Lumber Company’s 1920s sheds in Longview, Washington, were repurposed for the mansion. Some beams stretched over 75 feet, arriving weathered, studded with nails, and requiring extensive labor to re‑grade and remanufacture.Building a billionaire's dream homeGates purchased the land for his Medina property in 1988 for $2 million, and the following year ran an international architectural competition to find the right team to design it. Construction on the sprawling 66,000-square-foot Pacific Lodge-style home, later known as Xanadu 2.0, began in 1990 under architects James Cutler and Peter Bohlin. The original plan called for vast quantities of timber, much of it expected to come from some of the finest old-growth trees still standing.That plan ran headfirst into a national environmental reckoning. Around the same time construction began, the discovery of the threatened northern spotted owl triggered sweeping restrictions on logging old-growth forest habitat across the country. Cutler, known as one of the most environmentally committed architects in the Pacific Northwest, was firmly opposed to felling living old-growth trees for the project regardless of the restrictions.A billionaire chooses to compromiseRather than push back or seek workarounds, Gates opted to change course entirely. Cutler had been introduced to a Duluth-based salvaged-lumber dealer named Max Talbert, who suggested an alternative: building the mansion from reclaimed wood instead of freshly cut timber. Gates agreed, and went further than simply sourcing the material — he invested millions into a reclaimed-timber operation tied to Ferndale-based G.R. Plume & Company, according to a report in Architectural Record. In the process, Gates helped fund what Cutler described as the world's first heavy-timber-recycling sawmill, effectively catalyzing an entirely new market for salvaged structural lumber.Half a million board Feet of reclaimed historyThe wood that ultimately went into Xanadu 2.0 had a history of its own. It came from Long-Bell Lumber Company work sheds built in the 1920s in Longview, Washington, which had sat empty for nearly four decades before finally coming down in 1996. Roughly half a million board feet of timber from those sheds made its way into the Medina mansion, including reclaimed Douglas fir beams stretching more than 75 feet long. The salvaged material arrived in rough shape — weathered, inconsistently sized, studded with old nails, bolts, and spikes, and carrying no formal grading stamp.None of that made it a cheap shortcut. Reclaimed wood of this kind typically costs roughly three times more than standard timber, given the labor involved in de-nailing each piece, scanning for hidden metal, re-grading the material, and remanufacturing it into columns, beams, and trusses precise enough to meet architectural tolerances.An early signal of Bill Gates's environmental streakAt the time, sourcing an entire mansion's structural timber from reclaimed material at this scale was highly unusual. What began as a workaround for one high-profile home has since become an established practice across the architecture and hospitality industries, with hotel groups, restaurant designers, and high-end residential architects now routinely trading on reclaimed structural timber as a premium building material.In hindsight, the decision reads as an early marker of the environmental interests Gates would later pursue on a much larger scale — backing dozens of climate ventures through Breakthrough Energy Ventures, founding advanced nuclear energy company TerraPower, and commissioning Breakthrough, the world's first hydrogen-powered superyacht. Gates's $132 million Xanadu 2.0 today stands, quite literally, on timber salvaged because of a small, threatened owl species barely larger than a house cat — a detail that set off a chain of consequences few could have predicted at the time.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Steep rise in young UK nationals detained for smuggling drugs from Asia
articles.summary: Hundreds of Britons have been detained in Thailand on suspicion of attempting to smuggle cannabis to the UK.
articles.body:
The number of young British nationals arrested abroad after being recruited as drug mules more than quadrupled over three years, according to new government figures.

They showed a steep rise from just over 80 arrests in 2023, to more than 340 in 2025 - with the increase driven by cannabis-related offences linked to Thailand and elsewhere in South East Asia.

People are lured by gangs with the "promise [of] free travel or a quick way to make cash", said Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, who warned of harsh treatment if detained abroad.

Earlier this year, a BBC investigation found Thailand-based drug gangs were recruiting people to transport large quantities of cannabis in suitcases.

In some instances, people were told they would be carrying suitcases full of clothes, gold or cash. Instead, they contained up to 71kg of cannabis.

Cannabis is a Class B drug in the UK, with penalties of up to five years in prison for possession and up to 14 years for supply and production, as well as unlimited fines.

The Foreign Office said more than 200 British nationals have been detained on suspicion of smuggling cannabis from Thailand, a popular tourist destination. Since 2024, around 60% of them have been aged between 16 and 20.

Young people are commonly recruited on social media and are often incentivised to carry luggage for gangs without knowing its contents.

According to research commissioned by the Foreign Office, a third of young Britons surveyed did not consider travelling with luggage packed by someone else to be a risk.

Penalties for smuggling overseas include prison sentences, fines, corporal punishment such as whipping, or in some cases, the death penalty.

Doughty said "no holiday, payment or opportunity is worth risking your freedom, your future or your life".

He continued: "Detainees are warning about the dire living conditions they now face decades of in prison or, in some countries, the possibility of the death penalty."

One Briton detained abroad described a "sense of mourning for the life" they previously had, while another said: "It's your freedom you're risking, and once it's gone, it's not easy to get back."

Smuggling from Malaysia, Laos and Cambodia was also cited by the UK government as common smuggling sources, as it launched a campaign to deter young British nationals from transporting illicit cargo.

In July, the National Crime Agency (NCA) said British "mules" caught smuggling cannabis from Thailand would face prison, and would have to pay Thai Customs 30,000 Baht (£680) per kilogram to leave the country.

So far in 2026 there have been more than 160 cases of British nationals arrested overseas for drug smuggling offences, the Foreign Office said.

In 2024, police seized £13.8m worth of cannabis smuggled from Thailand at Birmingham Airport. Eight of the 11 people convicted for their involvement last month were in their twenties.

articles.title: Andy Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
articles.summary: The PM is understood to have cancelled engagements for Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is understood to have cancelled engagements for Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy.

Burnham has previously spoken about his father, who had Alzheimer's, when explaining why he was so determined to reform adult social care in England .

He also revealed his father did not know he had become prime minister in July, because of his condition.

The PM was due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street later.
